text:
JH-5108

SUPERIOR
COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-04-027629-014

DATE:

NOVEMBER 21, 2001

______________________________________________________________________

PRESENT:

THE HONOURABLE

MR. JUSTICE ALLAN R. HILTON

______________________________________________________________________

J... T...

Petitioner

vs.

L...-A... B...

Respondent

and

ATTORNEY
GENERAL OF QUEBEC

Mis en cause

______________________________________________________________________

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

I

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

On November 16, 2001 this Court issued an order,
with detailed reasons to follow, after four days of hearing on the Petitioner's
amended motion brought pursuant to
sections 18
,
19
and
39
of the
Act

respecting
the civil aspects of international and interprovincial child abduction
[1]
(
the

Act
)
, which is
the legislation in Quebec implementing the
Convention on the Civil
Aspects of

International Child Abduction
(
the

Convention
)

to which Canada was one of the original signatories. These are the  detailed
reasons for the issuance of the Order, which granted in part the Petitioner's
amended motion and ordered the return of the two children of the marriage to Los
Angeles, California.

II

THE FACTS

A)

The parties and the background

[
2
]

L...-A... B... was born in Montreal on [...],
1972. She moved with her mother to California in June of 1994, where she
obtained two graduate degrees, the last one of which was a Doctorate of
Psychology. J... T... was born in New Brunswick, New Jersey on [...], 1967. He
also moved to California in June of 1994 after having obtained two
undergraduate degrees from the University of Illinois and a Master of Public
Policy degree from Harvard University.

[
3
]

The parties were married in Chatworth,
California on June 13, 1995 after having met in San Francisco in 1994. They are
the parents of Le... D... T..., who was born on [...], 1998 and C... R... T...,
who was born on [...], 1999. Since their marriage, the parties have always
lived together in Los Angeles, and that is where their children were born.

[
4
]

For the last five years, until the events
described later in these reasons, the parties lived in a house at [...] in Los
Angeles, and from all appearances, they seem to have been very well integrated
into the Jewish community with a number of friends and acquaintances.

[
5
]

Ms. B... has spent most of her time looking
after the two children. She has not been employed in her chosen profession as a
psychologist because she lacks the post-graduate training that is necessary in
California for her to obtain her license to practise. Recently, however, she
began to teach on a part-time basis at the University of California at Los
Angeles.

[
6
]

It is not clear from the evidence what Mr. T...
does for a living, nor the extent of his assets. It is clear, however, that he
has accumulated what appears at first glance to be a staggering amount of debt,
both for business and personal reasons, and that he has borrowed significant sums
of money from a number of individuals, including his mother-in-law, Mrs. S...
K.... By way of illustration, the total of the two mortgages on the family
residence is in the range of U.S. $850,000, and his credit card liability is as
high as U.S. $215,000. In addition, as Ms. B... described it, the couple is
frequently "maxed-out" on various credit cards, and other family
members have had to help them out with the payment of day-to-day expenses.

[
7
]

Ms. B... has been particularly concerned with
the debt level of her husband since the birth of C…, around which time she
learned that her mother had loaned him U.S. $40,000, a fact that he had
concealed from her. Whatever the reality of his earning capacity and the extent
of his assets may be, it is obvious that Mr. T... has been unable to persuade
Ms. B... that he is able to provide for the family in light of his accumulated
debt. Ms. B... has also expressed her disappointment to Mr. T... about his
emotional commitment to her and to the marriage.

[
8
]

All of these circumstances, as well as
postpartum depression after the birth of her second son, led Ms. B... to seek
psychological assistance from a friend and former colleague in the early part
of 2000. This led to her being prescribed anti-depressant medication for several
months, however, her course on medication has now been discontinued.

[
9
]

A particular incident did occur during August of
2001 that does bear mention because of the way in which later events in October
transpired.

[
10
]

On August 22, Ms. B... left her husband and children
in Los Angeles for a brief stay in New York City without having previously
discussed the trip with Mr. T.... While her children were in a nearby park with
their nanny and Mr. T... was away from home, she delivered a note to the nanny
and asked her to give it to Mr. T.... The note indicated that she was headed
for New York City, that she could not handle the stress and had to get away.
The note did not say where she was going in New York City, although Ms. B...
did call Mr. T... the next morning to tell him she had arrived and would be
home in about four days.

[
11
]

When she returned to Los Angeles on August 26,
Mr. T... arranged a balloon-filled welcome home with notes from him and the
children telling her what a wonderful wife and mother she was. The family also
went out to dinner. While she was away, however, Mr. T... evidently panicked to
a certain degree, and he even went to the extent of filing a Missing Person's
Report with the Los Angeles Police Department that placed considerable emphasis
on Ms. B...'s alleged mental instability. She learned that he had done so
during a marital therapy session they were attending, and did not appreciate
his unflattering characterization of her mental status.

[
12
]

Ms. B... testified that she had told Mr. T... in
July this year that he had until October 1 "to get his act together",
or she would leave him. Unquestionably, what was paramount in Ms. B...'s mind
was her perception that the couple had enormous financial difficulties, and
that Mr. T... was unable to keep his end of the bargain of her staying home to
look after the children because he could not support her and them.

B)

The decision to leave Los Angeles for
Cambridge

[
13
]

It is in this context that discussions took
place in August and September for the family to leave Los Angeles for
Cambridge, Massachusetts where Mr. T... could take up a research fellowship for
the 2001-2002 academic year at the Harvard School of Business with an annual
stipend of U.S. $63,000. This opportunity was seen as a way to help put the
marriage back on track by a change of scenery in a pleasant university setting.
Doing so would also help relieve the couple of some of their imposing debt
obligations, since the idea was to sell the house and thus eliminate the huge
monthly mortgage payments, store the furniture, and live in subsidized
furnished housing on campus that would also include access to daycare
facilities. Mr. T... showed his wife floor plans of the accommodation they
could have in Cambridge, and indicated that final arrangements would be made
with the Housing Office at Harvard once they arrived in Cambridge.

[
14
]

The parties then began to put this plan into
action. They received an offer to purchase the house, and put it in escrow
while awaiting confirmation of the sale. They arranged for the storage of their
furniture (save for a few items such as the stove and a refrigerator that were
left in the house) in Los Angeles, notified their many friends of their plans
by electronic mail, and managed to cancel the children's attendance at a
daycare facility at no cost despite having signed a contract for an extended
period of time.

[
15
]

Ms. B... also began to seek employment
opportunities at Harvard, and prepared the itinerary for the long cross-country
drive, which included stops along the way at tourist sites such as Niagara
Falls and at the home of Mr. T...'s parents in Chicago.

[
16
]

It is apparent that Mr. T... and Ms. B... were
not leaving Los Angeles on a definitive basis, even though the precise date of
their return from Cambridge remained uncertain. Nevertheless, they would be
gone for at least the academic year ending on July 31. After moving everything
out on September 26, 27 and 28, the family stayed at the home of Ms. B...'s
mother on September 28, 29 and 30. They left Los Angeles on October 1 by car
and began heading east.

C)

The trip from Los Angeles to Cambridge

[
17
]

After a long trip that required staying in a
different hotel each night except when they were in Chicago, the parties and
their children arrived in Cambridge late on the evening of Wednesday, October
10. Despite the tourist activities that were undertaken as they travelled
across America, and the brief respite at the home of Mr. T...'s parents in
Chicago, Ms. B... found the voyage to have been a gruelling exercise. She
testified that she was exhausted and needed to rest. Her feeling in this regard
is easy to understand when it is remembered that she and her husband were
travelling a considerable distance with two very young children, the youngest
of whom, C…, was still in diapers.

[
18
]

The couple also learned as they were driving to
Cambridge that the potential buyer of their residence had withdrawn his offer
because of dissatisfaction with some of the physical elements of the house.
This meant that the financial burden of the huge monthly mortgage payments
would again raise its ugly head, as they had intended to pay the accumulated
mortgage arrears from the proceeds of sale.

[
19
]

Once they found out that the Housing Office
would not be open until the following Monday, instead of resting on Thursday,
October 11 and Friday, October 12, Mr. T... decided to embark on a search for
off-campus housing in the Cambridge area so as to keep the family's residency
options open. Ms. B... was troubled by this because if they leased premises,
they would have to pay rent in the range of U.S. $2,000 per month, on top
of the considerably higher mortgage payments in Los Angeles, without even
factoring in daycare expenses, the rest of their significant existing monthly
liabilities, and the cost of day-to-day living. In her mind, it simply did not
add up on Mr. T...'s gross salary of U.S. $63,000 per year. Moreover, she
did not understand why they were even bothering to look at premises off campus
if indeed they were meant to be living for free on campus.

[
20
]

In addition, she began to have doubts about
whether Mr. T... actually did have a fellowship because he kept making
telephone calls enquiring about its logistics. Coupled with the lack of housing
for them on their arrival, this raised doubts in her mind as to whether she was
being misled, and whether Mr. T... was simply buying time in an attempt to save
the marriage.

[
21
]

At lunchtime on Friday, October 12, she handed a
note to Mr. T... saying she did not want to visit any more rental premises that
day. Nevertheless, they returned that afternoon to a place that they had not
been able to see earlier. On the way back to the hotel, Mr. T... made a wrong
turn as they were heading towards a park. This seemingly minor incident upset
Ms. B... immensely in conjunction with the fact that she had just spent the
afternoon doing something she had told her husband she did not want to do.

D)

Ms. B...'s departure for Montreal

[
22
]

When they finally arrived at the hotel, she went
to the room to compose herself while Mr. T... parked the car. The children were
asleep in the back seat. She placed a telephone call to a former boyfriend in
Montreal to ask if she could come to Montreal with the children. She terminated
the call without completing it when Mr. T... arrived, and she hastily began
packing. She told Mr. T... that she was going to Montreal with the children.
She did not ask him what he thought of the idea. Rather, she announced it as a
statement of fact.

[
23
]

Mr. T... did not realize that Ms. B...'s plans
did not include him, because his reaction was to suggest that it might be a
good idea for the whole family to spend the weekend here, and that perhaps they
could discuss it in the car. She refused to consider the possibility of his
accompanying her and the children. She told him she was fed up with sleeping in
a different bed every night, and had to get away.

[
24
]

The couple went downstairs to check out. Ms.
B... withdrew U.S. $300 from an ATM machine, and retrieved the car while
Mr. T... was settling the account. The luggage was placed in the car along with
the children while he was still at the front desk. Ms. B... took off without
saying goodbye to her husband or allowing him to say goodbye to his children.
Her departure was so hasty, as it turned out, that she had even taken some of
Mr. T...'s clothing that she later had to have returned to a Greyhound Bus
Terminal in Boston.

[
25
]

Mr. T... was surprised to see his wife had left
him in this way. He called her mother in Los Angeles, her brother in Montreal
and another friend in Montreal to find out if they knew where she was going.
They too were unaware of Ms. B...'s plans.

[
26
]

Ms. B... exited the hotel parking lot by driving
the wrong way on a one-way street connecting to an entrance to the expressway.
She thus got lost on the way out of Cambridge en route to Montreal, and then
became stuck in traffic. After she was on the highway, she telephoned her
friend in Montreal to advise him that she was coming. He gave her the address
of a place to go to in the Montreal suburb of Côte St. Luc. She also tried to
reach Mr. T... on his cell phone without success.

E)

Events before the commencement of legal
proceedings

[
27
]

Finally, Ms. B... arrived here on Saturday,
October 13 at 2:00am after a long drive. She did speak to her husband in the
early hours of the morning to tell him that she had made it to Montreal safely,
that the children were all right, and that they would speak later that morning.
She did not tell him where exactly she was in Montreal, nor did he ask.

[
28
]

When they spoke on October 13, Ms. B... gave Mr.
T... a cellular telephone number at which he could reach her, and made it clear
to him that she would not be returning to Cambridge until Mr. T... had
accomplished three things: finding an address, a bed and a telephone number.
Mr. T... set about to do just that.

[
29
]

The next day, on Sunday, October 14, he signed
a lease for off-campus premises at an address in Cambridge for a term beginning
on October 15 and ending on July 31, 2002 at a monthly rental of
U.S. $2,200. Her signature, however, was required to finalize the
arrangement. He also initiated the process of having the premises furnished and
obtaining a telephone number.

[
30
]

On Wednesday, October 17, after Ms. B... had
been informed of these developments, she told Mr. T... that she would now
return. She asked him to wire-transfer her some money, as she had run out of
the cash she had taken from the ATM machine at the hotel in Cambridge before
she left on October 12. Mr. T... did send U.S. $250 that arrived on Saturday,
October 20, and Ms. B... told him she was heading for Cambridge that day. Mr.
T... stocked the refrigerator in the leased premises, and tried to arrange them
as best he could to welcome Ms. B... and the two children in a somewhat festive
manner.

[
31
]

At 7:30pm that evening, Ms. B... telephoned Mr.
T... and told him she had been forced to return to Montreal as she had been
refused entry into the United States at the border crossing in Phillipsburg,
Vermont because she did not have the children's birth certificates. Mr. T...
was stunned, as he had been under the impression that his immediate problem of
reuniting the family had finally been resolved.

[
32
]

He then called the United States Embassy in
Ottawa, and was referred to someone at the border crossing in Champlain, New
York (which is not on the most direct route between Montreal and Cambridge).
That person checked the log entries for Phillipsburg and told Mr. T... that
there was nothing to indicate that Ms. B... had been denied entry into the
United States. Mr. T... then explained his wife's dilemma concerning the
absence of birth certificates, and received information that he communicated to
her at 8:30pm that evening about what to do when she next came to the United
States border with the children. He even provided Ms. B... with the telephone
number of the officer at the border should she encounter any difficulty.

[
33
]

In fact, Ms. B... had not been denied entry to
the United States. She testified that when she was questioned by the officer at
the border who asked her for the children's birth certificates, she decided
that fate was telling her that her going to Cambridge was not going to work, so
she simply turned around and headed back to Montreal. Ms. B... acknowledged
that she did not attempt to persuade the officer that the two children were
indeed hers, as she had done with success when she crossed into Canada on the
morning of October 13 and had been confronted with the same inquiry from the
Canadian immigration officer.

[
34
]

The Court finds her account of events in this
respect to be implausible. If indeed her story is true as to what transpired,
that is not what she told Mr. T... when she telephoned him that evening. It is
also noteworthy that no one who was with Ms. B... while she was in Montreal,
such as her former boyfriend, was called as a witness to state that she had in
fact left Montreal on the afternoon of October 20. This is all the more
surprising since Ms. B... told Mr. T... the next day that she had been up until
the early hours of the morning after her supposed return to Montreal with her
former boyfriend, which she then used as an excuse not to drive to Cambridge on
Sunday, October 21 because she was too tired.

[
35
]

As a result of all of this, Mr. T... decided to
come to Montreal. He telephoned Ms. B... from Logan Airport in Boston in the
late afternoon to tell her he was coming, a fact that she did not greet with
any enthusiasm. Mr. T... suggested that they all might drive back the next day
and take advantage of seeing the tree colours change on the scenic journey
through Vermont on the way to Cambridge.

[
36
]

Ms. B... rejected this idea. He says she
launched into a verbal assault that amounted to a tirade about his
responsibility for their predicament. She said she had no intention of
returning with him to Cambridge. He found the tenor of this discussion to be
shocking.

[
37
]

Upon his arrival in Montreal, he checked into a
hotel and called his wife. They agreed to meet the next morning for breakfast
at a restaurant.

[
38
]

To Mr. T...'s surprise, Ms. B... did not have
the children with her when he arrived at the restaurant. He had not seen them
since October 12. From her perspective, this was appropriate since she felt
they had matters to consider concerning their marriage that could not be
discussed with the two young children present. In fact, Ms. B... had enrolled
them the previous week in a daycare facility in Hampstead not far from where
she was staying in Côte St. Luc.

[
39
]

The breakfast meeting lasted over two hours, and
covered three specific issues for which Ms. B... insisted on obtaining written
confirmation. She made it clear she would not leave without this, and that Mr.
T... would not be able to see the children until he gave her what she was
looking for.

[
40
]

First, Ms. B... expressed her concerns about her
own potential liability on the various debts Mr. T... had contracted in Los
Angeles. He reassured her that she had no personal liability because they were
all business debts for which he alone was responsible.

[
41
]

Next, she complained about his having questioned
her mental stability to various persons with whom he had spoken in Los Angeles,
including her mother, Ms. B...'s psychologist friend as well as her
psychiatrist. He agreed that she appeared to be in a normal frame of mind. In
her presence, he telephoned both the psychologist and the psychiatrist in Los
Angeles. He left voice-mail messages for both of them saying that he was with
Ms. B... at that very moment and that she was fine.

[
42
]

Finally, she wanted him to agree that he had
consented to her being in Montreal with the children. Although that was plainly
not the case, Mr. T... felt that unless he agreed to say he had consented, he
would not see the two children.

[
43
]

Mr. T... therefore provided Ms. B... with the
written confirmation she had requested. He did so on the back of a restaurant
placemat. In that part of the document that is of particular interest in these
proceedings, Mr. T... wrote as follows: "I am not objecting to L...-A...
having the kids in Montreal while I am not there. For the time being I consent
to L...-A... being with the kids in Montreal. If I change my mind I will inform
L...-A...."

[
44
]

With the written confirmation in hand that she
had requested, Ms. B... then took Mr. T... to see the children at the daycare
facility in Hampstead. Later that day, they together took the children to a
park in Côte St. Luc to play, and then to the residence where Ms. B... was
staying for a nap. The family had dinner together, and Mr. T... helped to bathe
the children and put them to bed. As Ms. B... declined his suggestion that he
stay the evening with her, he returned to his hotel.

[
45
]

The next day, Tuesday, October 23, also showed a
certain degree of civility in the relationship. Mr. T... arrived at Ms. B...'s
residence in the early morning, and the family had breakfast together. They
took the children to the daycare facility in Hampstead, and Ms. B... spent the
morning doing errands. Together, the picked up the children in the afternoon
and played with them. Following supper, the children were bathed and put to
bed, and Mr. T... returned to the hotel.

[
46
]

Wednesday, October 24, was for the most part
similar in nature in terms of the day's activities with the children. Mr. T...
had begun to feel good about the way things were progressing, and he believed
he had an agreement, albeit a fragile one, that Ms. B... would drive down to
Cambridge on Friday, October 26. Mr. T... decided to return to Cambridge that
evening, and did so by flying back to Boston.

[
47
]

On the evening of Thursday, October 25, Ms. B...
telephoned him in Cambridge and said she and the two children would not be
coming the next day. She told him that she had developed tonsillitis, and that
C… had an ear infection. During this conversation, which Mr. T... described as
a perfectly normal one, he told Ms. B... that he would return to Montreal and
drive everyone back to Cambridge. She agreed, and with her consent, he made an
appointment for a marital therapy session in Boston on the afternoon of Monday,
October 29.

[
48
]

None of this ended up happening.

F)

Events after the commencement of legal
proceedings

[
49
]

Instead, on Friday, October 26, Mr. T...
received an envelope from attorneys in Montreal delivered by Federal Express.
The envelope contained Superior Court of Quebec divorce proceedings
(500-12-260247-014) and separation proceedings (500-04-027429-014), along with
a motion for provisional measures and interim orders in the latter file in
which Ms. B... sought to be awarded custody of the children to the exclusion of
Mr. T..., as well as various forms of financial relief.

[
50
]

As a ground of divorce, Ms. B... alleged that
the parties would be separated for more than one year when the divorce judgment
would be rendered. Not surprisingly, she was unable to allege any facts that
would give this Court jurisdiction under
section 3
of the
Divorce Act
[2]
to grant a divorce. In the separation
proceedings, to establish jurisdiction under the
Civil Code of Quebec
,
she alleged that she was now domiciled in Montreal, and the ground asserted was
that the will of the parties to live together had been seriously damaged.

[
51
]

Mr. T... described himself as speechless in
light of what had transpired earlier that week. He telephoned attorneys in Los
Angeles.

[
52
]

The parties exchanged electronic mail
communications over the next several days, and spoke on the telephone as well.
Mr. T... also spoke with the children.

[
53
]

On Wednesday, October 31, Mr. T... initiated
divorce proceedings in the Superior Court of California, County of Los Angeles,
alleging irreconcilable differences as the ground of divorce. At the same time,
he obtained an
ex parte
order from Judge Richard E. Denner awarding him
"temporary physical care, custody and control" of the children,
subject to supervised visitation rights in favour of Ms. B.... Judge Denner
also ordered the parties to attend the Court's Custody and Mediation Service on
Wednesday, November 21 in Los Angeles.

[
54
]

In the meantime, Mr. T... came to Montreal to
begin the process of launching these proceedings. He and Ms. B... maintained a
civilized if somewhat strained relationship, and he continued to see the
children at the place where Ms. B... was staying in Côte St. Luc.

[
55
]

In addition to doing what was necessary to
initiate these proceedings, Mr. T... also enlisted the assistance of the
Attorney General of Quebec under the provisions of
section 10
of the
Act
.
On November 7, counsel on behalf of the Attorney General obtained an
ex parte

order from Coté, J. ordering the return of the two children to the Director of
Youth Protection. Essentially, the materials relied on by the Attorney General
were the original of Mr. T...'s motion in this case and those he had referred
to in the motion.

[
56
]

Mr. T... and Ms. B... had previously agreed to
meet for lunch on November 7 in the same restaurant where they had had
breakfast on October 22. Instead, while Ms. B... was there waiting for him, she
was served with the California divorce proceedings including the order of Judge
Denner, the order of Coté, J. that had been obtained by the Attorney General,
as well as Mr. T...'s motion in these proceedings. She also learned that the
two children had been removed by police officers from the daycare facility in
Hampstead and taken to an office of the Director of Youth Protection, where
they were subsequently given over to Mr. T.... The children remained with him
at his hotel in Montreal while the undersigned heard this case, save for
visitations with Ms. B... that the Court authorized and that took place without
incident on the evenings of November 12, 13 and 15.

III

ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION

[
57
]

Several of the requirements necessary to grant
the relief claimed by Mr. T... have been established without controversy. The
Government of Quebec has designated the United States of America as a
designated State under
section 41
of the
Act
, and the
Act

applies to the two children as they are under sixteen years of age as required
by
section 5
of the
Act
. Finally, it is not disputed that under
the law of California, both parents are equally entitled to the custody of
their children.

[
58
]

There are two principal issues to consider.

[
59
]

The first is whether Ms. B...'s removal of the
children to Montreal and her retention of them in Montreal was wrongful for the
purposes of
section 3
of the
Act
. This necessarily requires the
Court to determine whether it can refuse to order the return of the children
because Mr. T... consented or acquiesced to their removal or retention as
provided for in
section 21(1)
of the
Act
.

[
60
]

Second, the Court must establish what the
habitual residence of the children was when they were removed to Montreal, and,
if the removal occurred from a place other than their habitual residence,
whether it can return the children to the place of their habitual residence.

A)

Consent or acquiescence

[
61
]

There are several aspects to the issue of
consent or acquiescence raised on behalf of Ms. B... between the children's
departure on October 12 and the initiation of these proceedings on November 7.

[
62
]

There is no doubt that the manner in which Ms.
B... left her husband and took the children with her when she drove away from
the hotel in Cambridge could not even remotely be considered as one to which
Mr. T... consented. She simply told him she was going and left, leaving him
without all of his own luggage, and not even allowing him to say goodbye to his
children before she headed off down the wrong way of a street leading to an
entrance to the expressway. She obviously intended to leave as quickly as
possible, without debate or discussion, and categorically refused to have Mr.
T... accompany her.

[
63
]

When they finally spoke the next morning, she
set down the requirements for her return to Cambridge: an address; a bed, and a
telephone. This necessarily implied that her intention, as communicated to Mr.
T..., was that her stay in Montreal was temporary, and not permanent as she now
wishes it to be. In order to accommodate her desire to find housing, Mr. T...
did so without delay, which is a gesture on his part indicating without
equivocation that he wanted Ms. B... and the two children to return rather than
remain in Montreal.

[
64
]

Later that week, he responded to Ms. B...'’s
request to send her money to facilitate her return by car, and when she told
him she had been denied entry to the United States because she did not have the
children's birth certificates, which was not true, he immediately contacted
border officials to ascertain what needed to be done to have her cross the
border without incident. He gave her that information that evening, and asked
her to come down the next day, Sunday, October 21. When he spoke to her on
Sunday, she refused to come on the pretext that she was too tired.

[
65
]

It was then that Mr. T... determined that he
should come to Montreal, which he did that evening.

[
66
]

The conduct of Mr. T... between October 12 and
his arrival in Montreal on the evening of October 21 is consistent with one
objective: doing whatever he felt was necessary to persuade his wife to drive
with the children from Montreal to Cambridge, and completely inconsistent with
his consent or acquiescence to the children being in Montreal

[
67
]

Mr. T... remained in Montreal between the
evening of October 21 and the evening of October 24. During that time he met
and spoke with Ms. B... on several occasions, saw the children, and to a
limited extent tried to create as normal a familial situation as possible for
them under what were less than ideal circumstances.

[
68
]

Ms. B... places particular reliance on the
content of the document Mr. T... wrote out on the restaurant placemat as
referred to in paragraph [43] above. It will be seen immediately that the text
of that part of the document dealing with the children staying in Montreal with
their mother is neither unconditional nor permanent. On that basis alone, it
cannot be said to amount to an unqualified consent to the children being in
Montreal to begin with or an acquiescence to them remaining here.
[3]

[
69
]

In any event, this supposed consent cannot be
characterized as having been freely and voluntarily given. The Court has no
hesitation in concluding that by the morning of Monday, October 22, Ms. B...
had formed the intention not to return with her husband and their children to
Cambridge. Despite her testimony to the contrary, it seems evident from a sworn
statement signed by Ms. B... on November 8 that she had consulted counsel
before October 22, and that she understood she would be facing potential
difficulty in keeping the children here if she did not have some evidence of
Mr. T...'s consent. That must have been her purpose in inducing him to write
out what he did on the placemat.

[
70
]

The Court does not believe that Mr. T... was
fully aware of the truth of the matter when he signed what he did, and that Ms.
B... did not disclose in an accurate way what had transpired up until then, as
her admittedly inaccurate story about being denied entry to the United States
demonstrates. In the absence of full and complete disclosure, any supposed
consent given by Mr. T... was vitiated and cannot be enforced.

[
71
]

Moreover, his conduct subsequent to his return
to Cambridge on the evening of October 24 until his receipt of his wife's
proceedings on October 26 and the commencement of his own proceedings that were
served on Ms. B... on November 7 do not in any way show that he acquiesced to
his children remaining here on a permanent basis. He commenced the steps
necessary to assert his legal position on October 31 when he sought and
obtained an
ex parte
order in Los Angeles to have him awarded temporary
custody of the children, which accurately reflects his lack of consent to their
remaining in Montreal.

[
72
]

In addition, the Court places no credence on the
testimony of Ms. B... and her brother Br... that Mr. T... had begun to explore
job opportunities while in Montreal. He did see someone here in connection with
a work project, but that is a long way from seeking to secure employment, which
would subject him to Canadian and Quebec immigration requirements that it is
not obvious he would be able to meet.

[
73
]

Two other comments are warranted before moving
on to the next issue.

[
74
]

First, the fact that Mr. T... never told Ms.
B... that he did not consider the consent to have been validly given, or that
he did not mean what he wrote (such as it was), is entirely beside the point.
It cannot be forgotten that he had not seen the children for some ten days, and
that Ms. B... had made it clear to him she was not leaving the restaurant until
he signed what she wanted. He had little choice in the circumstances in order
to pursue his goal of reuniting the family in Cambridge.

[
75
]

Second, Ms. B...'s counsel argued that her
departure to Montreal from Cambridge and her decision to remain here were
warranted by the distrust generated by Mr. T... in terms of his financial
difficulties, her doubts about the truth of what she had been told about the
family's residential situation in Cambridge and his employment status at the
Harvard School of Business. During this time the mortgage on the home in
Cambridge was in arrears, and it was only after proceedings had begun here that
Mr. T...'s father wrote a cheque for U.S. $16,718.86 to satisfy the
arrears.

[
76
]

All of these concerns are proper ones in the
context of the merits of divorce proceedings. They can have no bearing,
however, on the issue of wrongful removal and retention of children, since the
only defences to a motion such as that of Mr. T... are those set out in
sections 21 and following of the
Act
. Justification of the type
argued on behalf of Ms. B... is not a defence mentioned anywhere in the
Act
.
Moreover, none of the other reasons under the
Act
that the Court
may refuse the return of the children, such as there being a grave risk that to
return the children would expose them to physical or psychological harm or
otherwise place them in an intolerable situation, have been alleged or argued.

[
77
]

The Court therefore concludes that the removal
of Le... D... T... and C... R... T... to Montreal was wrongful under the terms
of
section 3
of the
Act
, and that Mr. T... neither consented to
nor acquiesced in their removal or retention as contemplated in
section 21(1)

of the
Act
.

B)

Habitual residence

[
78
]

The concept of habitual residence is not defined
in the
Act
or the
Convention
. It is generally
understood that this omission is intentional, and that the framers of the
Convention

preferred to leave it to the courts to assess what the habitual residence was
of a child on a case-by-case basis without the constraint of a definition. The
exercise must necessarily be fact specific. The wisdom of that approach is
evident from the circumstances of this case, which appear to be unprecedented
in the case law.

[
79
]

Although counsel submitted authorities to the
Court from Quebec, Ontario, the United States, England and Israel, none of them
are even remotely similar to the facts of this case.

[
80
]

Our Court of Appeal has had the occasion since
1996 to canvass the question of how to determine a child’s habitual residence
on two occasions that counsel brought to the Court’s attention.

[
81
]

In
Droit de la famille – 2454
,
[4]
a Quebec couple decided to leave Quebec for
California in the summer of 1992 for financial reasons. The evidence was
conflicting as to whether the departure was meant to be temporary or permanent.
In any event, on December 31, 1992, United States authorities issued visas for
all members of the family that were good for three years. By the middle of
January of 1993, the family had moved all of their belongings to California. In
August of 1995, the wife obtained a work permit from the U.S. authorities, and
she landed a job there as a nurse. In December that year, the husband obtained
an extension of the visas for him and the children for three more years. In
January of 1996, however, the wife returned to Quebec with the children
unbeknownst to her husband.

[
82
]

In the Superior Court, Baker, J.
[5]
held that the children’s habitual residence
was California, and his judgment was confirmed by a majority of the Court of
Appeal (Chamberland and Forget, JJ.A., LeBel J.A. dissenting). In the course of
his reasons for the majority, Chamberland, J.A. endorsed the view that what was
important in a case of this nature in determining the habitual residence of
children was their reality at the time of their removal and not the intentions
of the parents when they both exercised custodial rights. That reality pointed
to California, not Quebec.

[
83
]

He also adopted the holding of Boggs, J. in the
case of
Freidrich v. Freidrich
,
[6]

decided by the Sixth Circuit of the United States Court of Appeals to the
effect that “habitual residence should not be confused with domicile”, and that
the determination of habitual residence required the court to “focus on the
child, not the parents, and examine past experience, not future intentions”.
Boggs, J. went on to note that a child can have only one habitual residence,
“which pertains to customary residence prior to removal”, and that the court
“must look back in time, not forward”.

[
84
]

Several important elements for a trial judge to
consider in determining the habitual residence of a child under the
Act

were enunciated by a unanimous bench of the Court of Appeal in
Droit de
la famille – 3713
,
[7]

including in particular that: “an appreciable period of time – one of a
duration necessary for the child to develop ties and to show signs of
integration into his new environment – should elapse before a new habitual
residence might be acquired”; that a “child should have a real and active
connection with the place of his residence”; and, finally, that for a residence
to be considered habitual, it “must have achieved a certain degree of
continuity”.

[
85
]

Applying these criteria to the circumstances of
this case, the Court concludes that the habitual residence of Le... D... T...
and C... R... T... when Ms. B... wrongfully removed them to Montreal on October
12 was Los Angeles, California and not Cambridge, Massachusetts, despite the
fact that the removal took place while the children were in the latter city.

[
86
]

They had been born in Los Angeles and had lived
there all of their short lives until they departed with their parents on
October 1. By the time they left Cambridge with their mother on October 12,
they had been there less than 48 hours and had spent two nights in different
hotels. They had not begun the process of integration into the Cambridge
community, and had spent the past few weeks travelling across the United States.
It is apparent that they had not been in Cambridge an appreciable amount of
time, that they had no real and active connection with Cambridge, and that
during their brief time there they had not achieved any degree of continuity,
let alone a “certain” degree of continuity.

[
87
]

At that particular time, the children’s reality
was in Los Angeles, and if they had been able to express an opinion on the
subject, even at their tender ages, the Court has no doubt they would have said
they lived in Los Angeles and not Cambridge.

[
88
]

In these circumstances, the Court must remain
free to return the children to Los Angeles, despite the fact that the removal
occurred while they were somewhere other than the place of their habitual
residence in Los Angeles. It would defeat the entire purpose of the
Act

and the
Convention
if a parent could successfully avoid their
application by the simple device of effecting the children’s removal while they
were not physically present in the place of their habitual residence.
Accordingly, that is why the Court issued its order on November 16 to return
the children with Mr. T... to Los Angeles.

C)

Reimbursement of expenses

[
89
]

There remains the question of reimbursement of
expenses that Mr. T... is claiming as provided for in
section 39
of the
Act
,
which the Court may order someone in the position of Ms. B... to satisfy “where
appropriate”. The Court left its determination of this claim until the release
of these reasons.

[
90
]

The purpose of this provision in the
Act

is plainly to act as a deterrent to wrongful removal and retention of children.
The Court is thus provided with a discretionary power that it must exercise
judicially.

[
91
]

Since his receipt of Ms. B...’s divorce and
separation proceedings on October 26, Mr. T... has been put to considerable
expense. He has come to and stayed in Montreal to initiate these proceedings,
engaged legal counsel who also prepared motions to decline the jurisdiction of
this Court in the two other court files referred to in paragraphs [49] and
[50]. He also spent time here for the four-day trial and at least the following
day when the Court’s initial order was issued on November 16.

[
92
]

That being said, and without in any way
condoning Ms. B...’s removal of the children in the manner revealed by the
evidence, it is improbable that she has the means to satisfy any monetary award
that the Court might otherwise be inclined to enter against her. It is equally
obvious that at least for the time being she is unemployed, and that until the
couple left Los Angeles her principal preoccupation was in looking after the
two young children. She too has incurred significant legal expenses in Quebec,
and more are on the horizon in Los Angeles, as she informed the Court she would
return there to defend her position before the Superior Court of California if
the Court granted Mr. T...’s motion.

[
93
]

In these circumstances, the Court concludes that
it would in the end only be harmful to the children of the marriage if Ms. B...
had to pay Mr. T... part of whatever liquid assets she is ultimately able to
lay her hands on. They would surely suffer at least to some extent by the
diversion of money from her to Mr. T.... Having heard Mr. T... testify, having
seen the lengths to which he has gone to secure the return of the children to
Los Angeles, realizing however that the costly legal battle for custody and
other matters in Los Angeles has only just begun, and knowing that both he and
Ms. B... want only the best for their children, the Court will exercise its
discretion in favour of Ms. B... and not order her to reimburse Mr. T...’s
expenses in connection with this litigation.

[
94
]

It will, however, amend the conclusions of the
initial order issued on November 16 to specify that Mr. T...’s amended motion
is maintained in part on the same terms, but with costs in favour of his
counsel only, the amount of which the Court knows will not be excessively
burdensome to Ms. B... under the applicable
Tariff
, but which
will serve as an adequate deterrent in the circumstances.

IV

DEFINITIVE ORDER

[
95
]

The Court maintains the amended motion of the
Petitioner J... T... in part, orders the return of Le... D... T... and C...
R... T... with their father J... T... to the place of their habitual residence
at [...], Los Angeles, California, dismisses the other conclusions of the
Petitioner’ amended motion, and orders provisional execution of the present
judgment notwithstanding appeal, with costs in favour of the Petitioner’s
counsel, but without costs in favour of counsel for the Attorney General of
Quebec.
